Dastardly Deed of a Delaware Darkey,
WILMINGTON. Del Feb. 25-A negro
WILMINGTON, Del. Feb. 25.—A negro called Jim Loat, alias Somers, was arrested at Middletown, Del., last night for a criminal assault upon the 14-year-old daughter of Henry Purse, a farmer, living near Odessa. There is much excitement in that vicinity, intensified by a general belief that justice miscarried in the Near case, and threats are made of summary punishment for the accused.

WILMINGTON, Del., Feb. 25.—An organized attempt has been made to lynch the negro Loat, but it was successfully resisted by the officers of the law, who took the prisoner safely to New Castle on the noon train and lodged him in jail there.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A4:
THE ODESSA OUTRAGE
NO NEW DEVELOPMENTS IN THE CASE—A PRELIMINARY HEARING BEFORE MAGISTRATE VAN DYKE.

There seem to be no new developments in the dastardly outrage that was committed near Odessa, on Thursday afternoon last, beyond those fully given in the GAZETTE of Saturday.

The licherous fiend was given a hearing at 9 o'clock on Friday evening before Esquire VanDyke, of Fdessa, at which the little victim of the foul deed, related, between her uncontrollable sobs, the story of the crime, and also positively identified the inhuman wretch.

Elias Pryor, colored, testified to seeing the prisoner at the door of the victim's father, as he was passing, the prisoner called to him saying: "Hello, old man." He could not be mistaken in the man.

Charles Bristor, colored, testified to seeing the prisoner approaching the house where the crime was committed. This completed the evidence and the prisoner was committed without bail.

While Deputy Sheriff Pennington waiting with his prisoner at Middletown for the train threats of lynching were fircely made and at one time it looked as though the threats would be carried into execution. The only thing that unfortunately prevented it was the moving off of the train.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A6:
ANOTHER BLACK FIEND.
A Leprous Negro Outrages a Little Girl Thirteen Years Old.
THE CRIME COMMITTED ON BISHOR SCOTT'S FARM.
The Fiend Captured After a Long Chase.
SAFELY LODGED IN NEW CASTLE JAIL
—THREATS OF LYNCHING—
DETAILS OF THE SHOCK-
ING CRIME.
THREATS OF LYNCHING
DETAILS OF THE SHOCK-
ING CRIME.

Encouraged, doubtless, by the acquittal of the negro, William Neal, on the charge of committing a hellish crime upon the person of Mrs. Margaret Gosser, of Blackbird Hundred, another black fiend, like a vulture, steps forth and emulates him, not upon the person of a woman but upon a little child.

When the facts of the crime became known a vigilance committee was at once formed and started in search of the foul fiend. After a search of many hours they succeeded in capturing him yesterday afternoon.

THE VICTIM.

The victim of the foul deed is a little thirteen year old daughter of Henry Perce, who resides in a tenant house on the farm of the venerable Bishop Scott, near Odessa. The fiend is a burly negro known by the name of James Loat, who was employed on one of the adjoining farms.
THE CRIME COMMITTED.

On Thursday morning last the father and mother of the victim, who are poor people, and obliged to eke out an existence by day's work, after bidding their daughter good bye and admonishing her to be careful, left what was at that time thier happy home for their respective places of labor. They departed in full confidence of the safety of their children, and little did they think at the time that a slimy snake would crawl into their happy home and sting their o dest daughter with its foul poison.

About 4 o'clock in the afternoon, the black fiend called at the home, and upon knocking, was answered by the daughter left in charge. He inquired for her father and being that he was not at home, put the same question in regard to her mother and received the same answer.

Being apparently satisfied that no one was at home to protect the defenceless girl, he boldly stepped into the house, despite all efforts of the daughter to prevent him. She at once attempted to give an alarm but was prevented from doing so by the fiend clapping one of his hands over her mouth. Even if she had been permitted to cry out, it would have been of no avail, as the house was
After having stopped the child's cries he, despite her struggles, threw her upon the floor and committed the fiendish crime.

THE ESCAPE.

After having accomplished the crime the negro fled, leaving his victim lying upon the flyor helpless. No one was present to help her in her helplessness. When her father returned from his day's labor she was sufficiently recovered to relate the circumstances, and give a description of the foul villain.

A VIGILANCE COMMITTEE.

The father almost dumbfounded and staggering under the great blow, started at once for Odessa, about 1½ miles away, to give the alarm. Arriving there he at once told his tale of woe to a party of men. A vigilant party was at once formed and after procuring a double team, attached to a large wagon, they started in pursuit and continued it until yesterday afternoon, when the villain was captured. The party with their prisoner at once drove to Odessa, and there being no other convenient place, the negro was confined in the cellar of Paullin's hotel, and guarded by a number of the men.

THREATS OF LYNCHING

Threats of lynching the black fiend were freely made, and it even went so far that a party was forming to do it, but some of the members backed out. Probably it might have been done had it not been for the arrival of Ash Pennington, Deputy Sheriff, who took charge of the prisoner. This morning Mr. Pennington brought his prisoner to New Castle on the train leaving Middletown at 11.07.

The victim is suffering greatly and is not expected to live.

This is the third crime of the kind that has occurred in that section of the county within a few years, two of the perpetrators being hanged and the third, (Neal), being acquitted. In order to have a salutary effect, some of the fiends should be strung up

THE REV. T. J. PRETTYMAN DEAD.—The Rev. Thomas J. Prettyman, pastor of the M. E. Church at Newark, Worcester county, Md., died suddenly on Monday afternoon. Mr. Prettyman was an industrious and earnest worker, and was somewhat noted as a revivalist. He was well-known in Pennsylvania and throughout the Peninsula. Two children of Mr. Prettyman recently died, and his sudden death adds another heavy blow to the stricken widow and daughter he leaves behind. Deceased was about 37 years of age.

ANOTHER OUTRAGE.—A Negro of Appoquinimink Commits an Unnamed Outrage upon a Little Girl.—Another of those detestable outrages called rape and which of late have become so painfully common in the lower part of New Castle co., was perpetrated by a negro on a little white girl in Appoquinimink Hundred about a mile and a half from Odaessa, on Thursday afternoon.

The name of the fiend who committed the outrage is James Redden, about 25 years of age and who resides with his father in a tenement house on the farm of Bishop Scott. The name of the victim of the negro's brutal passions is Sallie Purse, aged about 14 years daughter of William H. Purse, a respectable and respected citizen residing between Bishop Scott's farm and Odessa.

When the negro accomplished his fiendish purpose the family were absent from home except the girl and an infant. Information was given to the parents on their return home and the news being communicated to the neighbors a search was commenced for the negro who from the description given by the girl was believed to be Redden. The victim was terribly abused, but is much better. The search for the negro was kept up unremittingly and Friday evening he was arrested in J. D. Armstrong's store at Middletown.

Loud talk of lynching the villain was common in Middletown, and Constable Pennington who had the wretch in charge, had to use great precaution to keep his prisoner from being violently dealt with. On being taken before Esquire Vandyke, the little girl, who had been sent for, recognized him as the negro who had committed the outrage. Saturday morning Redden, in charge of Constable Pennington, was taken up to New Castle and lodged in jail to await trial at the May term of Court.

Redden though young, is an acknowledged outlaw. He is charged with having some two years ago decoyed a tramp into the woods near Middletown, where he assaulted, robbed him and left him for dead. He got clear through insufficient proof of the crime.

In an altercation with his father that morning, whose head he cut with a knife, he was shot in the wrist where the ball still remains. He claims he can prove an alibi.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A8: THE dastardly outrage committed by "Jim" Redden upon a white girl, in the neighborhood of Odessa, is fully reported in another column. A few months ago, when William Neal, upon whom was proven a clear case of rape, was turned out unpunished upon society, it was predicted that similar outrages upon defenseless white women would speedily follow, and the predictions were well founded. The outrage is one of the most nefarious of its kind ever committed in this State, and that its perpetrator was not promptly strung up on a limb of some handy tree to kick at indefinite space, speaks strongly for the forbearance of Odessa people, and proves that they have not lost all faith in the courts of their State. The evidence against Redden seems overwhelmingly conclusive, and he will doubtless be promptly tried, convicted and executed. Should his neck be saved by such means as were resorted to in the case of the negro Neal, no remedy will be left the people for the protection of their wives and daughters but a resort to the Court of Judge Lynch.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A9:
The Odessa Outrage.
little more than a mile from the
A little more than a mile from the town of Odessa, on the road leading to Fieldsboro, and at the gate of Mr. George L. Townsend, there lives in a small one story tenement house, Henry Purse, his wife and two children. The family is poor, and Purse is much away from home at labor. The eldest child, Sarah, is a bright, intelligent girl, about 14 years old, though, being of slight stature, she does not appear to an observer to be more than thirteen. The younger child is about three years old. On Thursday afternoon of last week, whilst Purse was away at work in the neighborhood of Snyrna, and Mrs. Purse at the house of a neighbor, the two children being alone, James Redden (alias Loat), a worthless negro of notorious character, entered the house and committed a felonious outrage upon the oldest girl. The details of such crimes cannot be printed in a decent newspaper, and decent people have no desire to read them. The child was left bruised, stunned, and frightened almost out of her wits. The condition in which her mother found her upon returning home attested to the fearful manner in which she had been mal-treated by the black-hearted as well as black-skinned and beastly scoundrel. Her husband being absent, Mrs. Purse hardly knew what to do, upon first learning of the outrage, but finally decided to go to Fieldsboro and ask the advice of Henry Willard. He advised her to say nothing further of the outrage until her husband returned. Mr. Purse came home late Friday evening, but in the meantime rumors of the outrage had reached Odessa and a search was being made for the villain. The girl did not know her assailant, and a clue to his identity was obtained through Charles Bristor, a negro, who, while coming from Fieldsboro, saw Redden at a window of Purse's house. This occurred, it is believed, before the assault was committed. Obtaining this important information from Bristor, Alexander Moody and Alfred Stevens went in search of Redden, found him in front of J. G. Armstrong's store, and secured him. He was then taken to Purse's in a carriage but was not taken in the presence of Sarah until she had given a detailed description of her assailant. Redden corresponded exactly to her description, even to that of a large ring upon one of his fingers. Being taken before her she instantly recognised him as the man who had assaulted her. He was then taken back to Odessa and confined in a room in Paullin's Hotel. There was no movement to lynch him, as reported by Wilmington reporters who sat in Wilmington and wrote up the details of the affair, "hit or miss." The quiet and order-loving people of Odessa seemed to have faith that the villian would get a just amount of hanging by due process of law. Deputy Sheriff Ash Pennington went to Odessa early Saturday morning and took charge of Redden. He was taken before Esquire Vandyke, who after hearing the testimony of the victim of the outrage, and Dr. Woods, and two colored men—Bristor and Frisby Lloyd—who saw the prisoner at the house of Purse, held him for court. Ash Pennington brought him to Middletown after the hearing and took him to New Castle on the 11 o'clock train. He is now behind the bars, and, it is said, has gone to praying loudly for his soul. The reports in the Wilmington papers that an attempt was made at Middletown to lynch the villian are utterly without foundation. If Middletown people had undertaken the job they would have carried it through. Redden is a negro of notorious reputation. A few years ago he nearly killed a white boy without the least provocation, but by some means escaped punishment.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A10:
An Atrocious Crime.
One of the atrocious crimes known to the calendar, is charged to have been committed by a colored man, known as James Redden, near Odessa, Delaware, on Thursday of last week. The facts as given are as follows: Upon the day named, Redden, who also owns the alias of "Loot," visited the house of Henry Purse, on the suburbs of the village of Odessa, during the absence of all the adult members of the family.

Purse's fourteen year old daughter was at home tending the younger children when the negro arrived. After ascertaining that the girl's parents were absent, the villain caught her by the arms and, stifling her mouth, committed a beastly assault. The child's father returned, and ascertained from the neighbors that the man had been in the neighborhood, but none had guessed the repulsive nature of his errand. The girl, when questioned, related the circumstances to her father, and the news of the crime spread through the town rapidly, and the citizens were frenzied with indignation and excitement. A warrant was sworn out for Redden's arrest, and he was taken into custody while entering a store in Odessa.

THE OUTRAGED CITIZENS GATHER.

He was confined in a private house over night, and an organized band of men visited the place for the purpose of lynching the negro, but his place of concealment could not be ascertained. The next morning he was removed from the house to the depot, and but for the timely arrival of the train which carried him to New Castle jail, he would have been mobbed—the band of lynchers ran madly to the train, too late to secure the prisoner. Redden is now confined the New Castle jail, and stoutly denies the charge upon which he is held. The negro is positively identified by the outraged girl and two neighbors who saw him in the vicinity of the house. The girl suffers severely, and it is feared is seriously injured by the rufian, and the event has caused the greatest excitement in the neighborhood.

Redden is the same individual who was some time ago arrested on the charge of assaulting and badly beating a pedlar, and shortly afterward attempting to kill his own father, escaping with little or no punishment in both cases.

jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A12:
Democratic Hypocrisy.
From Middletown Transcript.

Two of the Wilmington evening papers rather overdid themselves in the way of sensation in reporting the Odessa outrage. Readers would have a better opinion of newspapers if they would get the facts in such cases and stick to them. There was no attempt made here to lynch Redden, and probably not a dozen persons in Middletown knew that he was to be taken to New Castle on the noon train of Saturday. There was no unusual crowd at the station, and there was not the least disposition shown to open court with Judge Lynch on the bench. Had the circumstances of his atrocious crime and the fact that he was to be taken to New Castle on the train been generally known here, the state of affairs at the station might have been more exciting. But perhaps it is best as it is.

The two evening papers alluded to in the above article were the Democratic Every evening and Gazette, and the articles were no doubt penned by their young and enterprising reporters.
jim-loaf-middletown-1882-02-25.A17:
THE GALLOWS.
JAMES REDDEN PAYS THE
DEATH PENALTY OF
VIOLATED LAW.
THE CRIME.
THE CRIME.

The crime for which James Redden suffered the extreme penalty of the law was committed on the morning of the 23d of last February. His victim, little Sallie Purse, who was then about 13 years of age, being alone in the house, with the exception a baby sister, about 2 years of age. The house where the outrage was committed, is situated on the road between Odessa and Fielssboro. The father had been away for a couple of days, and the mother had gone that morning, immediately after breakfast, to see a sick person, leaving Sallie to wash the dishes and straighten up the house. About 9 o'clock Redden came along and after entering the house asked the girl to give him something to eat. Not having anything cooked she baked him some cakes, fried some meat and made some coffee. When he was done eating he went to the door and after looking up and down the road returned, and seizing hold of the child threw her on the floor, at the same time telling her "if you holler, I'll kill you," accompanying the threat with a motion as though he was about to draw a knife from his pocket.

THE ARREST.

After the foul death had been consummated he remained in the house for several hours, and then threatening her with death in case she told her mother, he took his departure. While he was in the house two colored men passed along the road and he spoke to one of them. When Mrs. Purse returned in the evening, Sallie told her what had happened but it was some time before the mother could believe it. The next day Mr. Purse returned, but before he reached home heard of the affair which by that time was pretty well known all over the country. The father had a warrant issued immediately, and Redden was arrested the same evening while holding a horse in front of Vandyke's store. He was taken to the house of Mr. Purse, and fully identified by Sallie as her assailant. The next day he was taken to New Castle where he was kept until the May term of Court when he was brought to this city for trial.

THE TRIAL AND CONVICTION.

When the case was called Harry Sharpley, Esq., was appointed by the Court to defend him. After a delay of several days, during which Mr. Sharpley was using every means in his power to obtain witnesses who would be able to clear his client of the horrid crime with which he was charged the trial was commenced.

The prisoner plead not guilty, and after some fifteen challenges had been made a jury consisting of 11 white men and 1 colored man was secured. The evidence was direct and convincing, that of his victim, who broke down several times on the stand, especially so. The defence endeavored to prove an alibi, but utterly tailed in the attempt and the few witnesses that were examined only tended to show still further that he was at the house the time the offense was committed. The counsel on both sides made able arguments, and the jury after being charged by the Chief Justice, retired at noon on the second day of the trial. The evidence was so clear that it was not expected they would be out more than a few hours, but contrary to all expectation it was 19 hours before they arrived at a verdict. They came into Court on the morning of the second day for instructions, and about an hour afterwards returned with a verdict of guilty. Immediately after the verdict was rendered Court adjourned until 3 o'clock in the afternoon. During the recess the prisoner was removed to one of the cells in the basement of the Court House, and made no hesitation in confessing his guilt and saying that all the girl had said was true.
At 3 o'clock in the afternoon of the same day he was again brought into Court and the Chief Justice after dwelling on the enormity of the crime, and picturing the blasted life of this innocent child, sentenced him to be hung on the 25th of August.

HOW HE PASSED THE TIME.

After his sentence he was removed to New Castle jail in a close carriage. He has been quiet and orderly, and ate his meals with a relish that seemed strangely in keeping with the position in which he was placed. He was frequently visited by Rev. Dr. Spotswood, a colored preacher and other friends. He learned to read and seemed to take great pleasure in reading the Bible. His mother is a constant visitor and has always tried to give him encouragement and consolation. Although she always seemed calm an observer could not fail to see that it was only by a great effort she concealed her emotions while she was in his presence. On several occasions he has confessed that he did wrong and was sorry for it.

THE EXECUTION.

Redden was executed at 10.21 this morning. The Sheriff cut the rope and his feet touched the ground. At 10.26 the movement of the heart ceased.

THE NEGRO REDDEN, WHO COMMITTED A RAPE ON A LITTLE GIRL, HANGED TO-DAY.
NEW CASTLE, DELI August 25 James Redden
THE NEGRO REDDEN, WHO COMMITTED A RAPE ON A LITTLE GIRL, HANGED TO-DAY.

NEW CASTLE, DEL., August 25.—James Redden, the negro hanged here to-day for rape on a 12-year old white girl, named Sallie Purse, near Odessa, last February, passed a very restless night, praying and walking the floor, until 3 o'clock this morning, when he fell asleep and rested for an hour and a half. For breakfast he ate beef, fried eggs, bread and milk, and ice cream. He wept at times during yesterday and last night. Yesterday afternoon he was visited by two clergymen, who spent half an hour with him. His mother, who was to have visited him yesterday, failed to arrive. From 9 o'clock this morning up to the hour of his execution Redden was closeted in his cell with the Revs. Nicholas M. Brown, of New Castle, and Wesley J. Parker (colored), pastor of Ezion M. E. church, Wilmington. They prayed with him, and he joined, in a steady voice, in singing "Salvation's Free" and several other hymns. At 10:12 the prisoner, preceded by the Rev. Mr. Brown, and followed by the Rev. Mr. Parker, Warden Hance, Sheriff Clark and his son, George Clark, ascended the scaffold with a firm step and took his place on the trap. Rev. Parker offered up a short prayer, after which the noose was adjusted, the black cap drawn over the prisoner's face, his ankles pinioned and, without saying a word to those assembled, he was launched into eternity at 10:17. He died easily of strangulation in 11 minutes. The execution was witnessed only by the officers of the jail, two physicians, two clergymen, the jurors and press representatives, and one woman who manifested a strong disposition to see a man hung.

The following is a history of the case: James Redden, who was also known previous to his arrest as "Jim Loat," was a full-blooded negro, about 21 years old, and slightly under the medium stature. His face was beardless and somewhat stupid and sullen in its habitual expression. He had lived around Odessa, in the central part of this county, most all his life, and had earned a reputation for general good-for-nothingness and an ugly disposition. Besides some petty offenses, he was charged with having, some two years ago, decoyed a drunken tramp into the woods, robbed him and beaten him in a dangerous manner. On Thursday, February 231, of the present year, Redden entered the house of Henry Purse, a tenant of the late Bishop Scott, one-and-a-half miles below Odessa, during the absence of Purse and his wife, who had gone out to their daily labor learning the
entered the house of Henry Purse, a tenant of the late Bishop Scott, one-and-a-half miles below Odessa, during the absence of Purse and his wife, who had gone out to their daily labor, leaving the house in charge of their daughter Sallie, a girl of between 12 and 13 years. Sallie and her baby sister were the only inmates. The negro asked the little girl for something to eat, which she prepared and set before him. Having eaten, he lingered in the house for three hours, and during that time forcibly outraged Sallie, who resisted with all her feeble strength. Redden was arrested in Odessa the evening of the following day, with some difficulty gotten out of town, and lodged in New Castle jail on Saturday morning. Threats of lynching were made, public reeling being intensified by the memory of the Neal case, but the crowd lacked a leader.

On the 24th of May, the case was called for trial in the court sitting in this city, and, after some delay, a jury was empanneled, made up of eleven white and one colored men, the latter being the first negro juror who ever sat in a capital case in this state. Harry Sharpley, esq., was assigned by the court as counsel for the prisoner, and he entered into the defense so earnestly as to draw from some of his party (the democratic) unfavorable criticism for excess of zeal. But the evidence was too strong to be shaken, and the jury, after deliberating twenty-four hours, and balloting sixteen times for a verdict, found the prisoner guilty in manner and form as indicted. Redden listened to his trial and the sentence which followed close thereafter with stolic indifference, and did not seem to the observers to realize that his life had been forfeited. While awaiting his execution he maintained the same dogged indifference to his approaching doom, rarely referring to it, and still more rarely exhibiting any emotion. He was visited several times by his mother and sister, and frequently by members of the New Castle clergy, both white and colored, in whose conversation and prayers he seemed to take much comfort. He talked freely about his crime, but always stoutly maintained that it was nothing more than seduction, and that he committed no assault.
